FloppyData is the cheapest NetNut replacement on this site: a flat $1/GB for rotating residential, mobile and datacenter traffic, and static residential IPs from $1.79 each in monthly bundles, which covers NetNut's two core products. The caution is that it is a young provider with disputed pool-size claims and mixed reviews, which matters after a sourcing scandal like NetNut's. Use the vetting checklist on this page, test your targets, and keep critical workloads on a more established provider until FloppyData proves itself.

Former NetNut users looking at FloppyData are usually after the cheapest possible replacement. NetNut's domains were seized by the FBI on July 2, 2026, after Google linked its residential network to the Popa botnet. FloppyData offers residential, mobile and datacenter traffic at a flat $1/GB on one balance, plus static residential IPs from $1.79 each. This page explains NetNut's status, compares FloppyData with what NetNut offered and covers what to check before moving.
What happened to NetNut?

NetNut stopped being a normal buying option on July 2, 2026. That day the FBI and IRS Criminal Investigation seized NetNut-related domains, and Google published research linking the network's residential exit nodes to the Popa botnet, which it estimated at two million or more hijacked home devices. NetNut's parent, Alarum Technologies, rejects the allegations, but its main domains went on to show seizure banners and its share price fell sharply. Whatever the final legal outcome, routing business traffic through that infrastructure now carries legal and reputational risk.

blocks.text: FloppyData in 2026: what you get

FloppyData is a young budget provider registered in Dubai that launched around 2024. Its pitch is radical simplicity: one balance at a flat $1/GB that you can spend on residential, mobile or datacenter rotating traffic, plus static residential and datacenter IPs sold in monthly bundles. Its residential page lists home ISP IPs in 148 countries and 442 cities. The company also offers a free cloud anti-detect browser that runs on its proxies. Its advertised 65M+ IP figure has been questioned by some reviewers, and user reviews are mixed.

FloppyData sells proxies the way prepaid phone plans sell minutes: one flat $1/GB balance that works across residential, mobile and datacenter pools. Static residential IPs start at $1.79 each in monthly bundles (20 for $49) with unlimited bandwidth. It is one of the cheapest ways into residential traffic, but it is a newer brand with less independent benchmarking than the established names.

Strengths: Flat $1/GB on any volume; One balance across residential, mobile and datacenter; Cheap static residential bundles with unlimited bandwidth; Free cloud anti-detect browser. Weak spots: Newer brand with limited independent testing; Pool-size claims disputed by some reviewers; Mixed customer-support reviews.
What NetNut offered, and how FloppyData compares

Before the seizure, NetNut was best known for ISP-sourced static residential proxies and a fast rotating residential network aimed at scraping, ad verification and brand-protection teams. Its residential rates generally ran from about $1.87 to $3.53 per GB on larger plans, with higher effective prices on entry plans. FloppyData covers much of the same ground: static residential (from $1.79/ip), static datacenter (from $0.79/ip), cloud anti-detect browser sit alongside its residential network, which advertises 65M+ claimed (disputed) IPs in 148 (residential) countries.
What former NetNut customers need, and whether FloppyData
delivers

Most NetNut accounts were built around three things: static ISP IPs for long-lived sessions, rotating residential traffic with US state and city targeting, and high concurrency for scraping. On static ISP-style IPs, FloppyData's answer is yes; its other products are static residential (from $1.79/IP), static datacenter (from $0.79/IP), cloud anti-detect browser. On rotating residential targeting, FloppyData offers country and city in 148 (residential) countries, with rotating or sticky sessions. Map each of your old NetNut zones to one of these before you migrate, so nothing breaks on the day you switch.
FloppyData pricing

FloppyData charges a flat $1/GB for rotating traffic, and the same balance works for residential, mobile and datacenter IPs. Static residential proxies are sold in monthly bundles from $1.79 per IP (20 IPs for $49), and static datacenter IPs from $0.79 per IP. Quick cost check for FloppyData: 10 GB comes to $10 ($1/GB), and 100 GB comes to $100 ($1/GB). NetNut's larger plans used to run about $1.87-$3.53/GB, so compare against what you actually paid rather than NetNut's headline rate.
How to migrate from NetNut to FloppyData
1. Export your NetNut usage history and list the countries, cities and session types you actually used, so you can map them to FloppyData's targeting (country and city).

2. Test before you commit. FloppyData's testing option: no free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations. Run your real targets for a day on the smallest purchase before moving production traffic.
3. Swap the gateway host and credentials in your scraper or browser profiles. FloppyData supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5.
4. Compare success rate, response time and cost per successful request against your old NetNut baseline, then move traffic over in stages.
5. Remove any NetNut SDKs, browser extensions or endpoints from your systems, and rotate any credentials that were stored alongside them.
Where FloppyData fits best
General web scraping: workable. Why: cheap, but with limited independent benchmarking.
SERP and rank tracking: workable. Why: workable for light tasks.
Social media and multi-account management: strong fit. Why: cheap static residential IPs and a free anti-detect browser.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: workable. Why: city targeting at a flat rate.
Ad verification and geo-testing: weak fit. Why: limited targeting depth and published data.
Tight budgets: strong fit. Why: a flat $1/GB on any volume.
Protocols and sessions

FloppyData supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5 and offers rotating or sticky sessions. Targeting covers country and city across 148 (residential) countries. Like NetNut's residential gateway, it works through a single backconnect endpoint with location and session options passed in the username, plus IP whitelisting.
How to vet a residential proxy provider after NetNut

The NetNut case showed that a residential pool can look like a normal enterprise product while resting on devices whose owners never meaningfully agreed to share their connection. Before you move traffic to any provider, including FloppyData, ask a few direct questions and keep the answers on file:
How are residential IPs sourced? Look for an opt-in SDK or app programme with clear user
consent and compensation, and ask which partner apps are involved.
Does the provider publish an ethics or sourcing policy, and has it been audited or certified (for
example AppEsteem or ISO 27001)?
What KYC does the provider apply to customers, and which target categories are restricted?
Strict onboarding is a good sign, not an inconvenience.
How does it handle abuse reports, and is there a named legal entity and jurisdiction behind the
service?
Can you get contractual assurances, such as a data-processing agreement, if your compliance
team needs them?
Bottom line

NetNut is no longer a provider you can plan around, so the real decision is which network replaces it. FloppyData is strongest for small budgets and experiments and multi-account work using the free cloud browser, starts at $1/GB flat, and offers no free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations. Test it on your own targets for a day, compare cost per successful request with your old NetNut baseline, and move production traffic in stages.

Small budgets and experiments
Multi-account work using the free cloud browser
Buyers who want residential and mobile without separate plans
